name: Dinghy Spark
geological_features: Electrostatic dust that levitates above the surface in the terminator zone
Smooth basalt plains with almost no topographical variation
A single large impact crater occupying the southern hemisphere
specific_features: Piezoelectric mineral deposits that generate visible electrical discharges when stressed by thermal cycling
description: Dinghy Spark is a tiny barren body barely large enough to have pulled itself into a roughly spherical shape, its surface a monotonous expanse of dark basalt broken only by a single impact crater that dominates the southern hemisphere. The body's most notable feature is the electrostatic activity in the terminator zone, where the temperature transition between the sun-baked day side and the frozen night side causes fine regolith particles to levitate and drift in ghostly clouds above the surface.

The piezoelectric mineral deposits add a second layer of electrical activity — as the surface undergoes thermal expansion and contraction during the day-night cycle, the minerals generate visible electrical discharges that arc between rock formations in brief, bright flashes. The effect is most dramatic at the terminator, where thermal stress is greatest, creating a moving band of tiny lightning bolts that circles the body with the day-night boundary. From orbit, the sparks give the planetoid a faint, flickering aura.

Dinghy Spark was cataloged as unremarkable until a prospecting vessel noticed the electrical activity during a close approach. The piezoelectric minerals are of moderate scientific interest but no significant commercial value, and the body's tiny size and negligible gravity make any surface operations awkward. It remains a curiosity, visited occasionally by survey teams studying electrostatic phenomena in low-gravity environments.

The name was applied by the prospecting crew who discovered it — their ship was a small, battered freighter they called the Dinghy, and the sparking surface seemed like a personal message. The name stuck in the charts, and Dinghy Spark has become a minor waypoint for vessels transiting the outer system, its flickering terminator a welcome sign of something happening in an otherwise empty stretch of space.
